Keywords: House of Warenne Chequy Or Azure
John de Warenne Earl of Surrey
RagShortTexts: The House of Warenne flew the gold-and-blue chequy banner, anchoring royalist defense at Lewes.

Variants.Content: The gold-and-blue chequy shield of the Warennes dates back to the Conquest, and the family's earls of Surrey held Lewes Castle as their seat in Sussex. John de Warenne married a half-sister of Henry III, and that marriage tied him closely to the royal house. In the crisis of 1258 to 1265 he became one of the most determined royalist opponents of Simon de Montfort's reform councils, and he insisted that his lands were held by the right of the sword rather than by any council's grant. His castles and retinues kept the Channel crossing open for royal reinforcements, and his wealth in land and knights made him a pillar of the loyalist cause. Every royal writ that touched Sussex was measured against his power to enforce it.

Warenne was proud and unyielding, and he kept seasoned retinues in Sussex ready to answer any summons. His couriers rode across the Channel with news for the royal household, so reinforcements could be planned and paid for without delay, and every mile of that road was counted in the earl's accounts.

The blue-and-gold chequered pennant stands over Sussex downlands, and village folk know its meaning. Warenne patrols ride the lanes at dusk, and they break up any gathering in the taverns that sounds like anti-royal sedition. Mail and spurs are checked at every gate, and a man who speaks against the king may find himself hauled before the earl's bailiff by morning.
